In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (1) What are the effects of different follow-up techniques on return rate?
the following question: How can a mail survey of pharmacy practitioners, pharmacy faculty, or pharmacy school alumni be designed to maximize the number of responses?
the following question: what is the effectiveness of follow-up techniques in increasing the return rate of mail surveys?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the most effective follow-up technique for increasing survey return rates in pharmacy surveys is to mail a second survey to all nonresponders.
a second mailing to nonresponders in a mail survey of pharmacy practitioners, school alumni, or school-based educators is associated with significantly higher survey return rates.

a second mailing of a mail survey to nonresponders is effective in increasing response rates, regardless of the type of survey population, the size of the survey sample, the type of follow-up techniques used and the geographic scope of the survey.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a second mailing of a survey to nonresponders is a good follow-up strategy for mail surveys of pharmacy practitioners and faculty members.
a second mailing of a survey instrument to non-responders is the only follow-up technique that is consistently associated with higher return rate.
follow-up techniques are not a panacea for low response rates in mail surveys.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single mailing is not likely to produce the highest response rates.
the most effective follow-up strategy is a second mailing of your survey.

a single mailing of the questionnaire to the entire sample of potential respondents is unlikely to yield a satisfactory return rate in most cases, and a follow-up mailing is essential for maximizing return rates.
